quote: the small vessel of my spirit
note: The poem as a sea voyage, an image ancient poets used for their own work. Dante's Italian says the little ship of his "ingegno": his talent, his poetic gift.
Hell, which Dante and Virgil left at the end of the Inferno by climbing from the center of the earth to its far side.

context: Everyone here is saved. The souls suffer to be made clean, not to be punished forever, and every one of them will reach Heaven.

quote: Let poetry rise from the dead
note: Dante's Italian says "dead poetry": the poetry that has been singing of the dead in Hell. It rises again here, on the morning of Easter Sunday, the day of the Resurrection.

context: The Inferno also called on the Muses near its start. The prayer here is longer and names one of them.

note: The chief of the nine Muses, and the Muse of epic poetry.

The nine daughters of King Pierus challenged the Muses to a singing contest. Calliope sang for the Muses and won, and the losers were turned into magpies for their boasting. The story is in Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book 5.
The deep blue of the sky before sunrise. It is the first color in the poem after the darkness of Hell, and the first open sky.

The morning star, rising before the sun. Dante names her only as the planet that moves us to love. Astronomers point out that at Easter 1300 Venus was in fact an evening star. Dante wanted her here: love presides over this realm.
A way of telling the time. The sun is in Aries, and Pisces rises just before Aries, so it is an hour or more before sunrise.

Usually read as the four cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance, the virtues open to all people, pagans included. Some have wondered whether Dante had heard of the Southern Cross. In Canto 8, three other stars take their place at evening, for faith, hope and charity.
Adam and Eve. The Garden of Eden is at the top of this mountain. After they were driven out, in Dante's geography, all humankind lived in the northern hemisphere, where these stars can't be seen.
The inhabited northern half of the world, which has lost sight of these stars. As allegory: humanity since the Fall has lost the perfect virtue it had in Eden.
The Big Dipper, the best-known constellation of the northern sky. From this far south it is below the horizon.

context: He is never named in this canto, only identified by his death at Utica. He died at 48. Dante makes him an old man, with the uncut hair and beard that the poet Lucan says he wore in mourning for Rome's civil war.

note: The four virtues shine so fully on Cato's face that he looks lit by the sun, the poem's usual image for God. He is the picture of the best a person could be by natural virtue.
Hell. Cato sees two figures who have come up from below and takes them for damned souls escaping.
The little stream that runs down a dark passage from this shore to the center of the earth. Dante and Virgil climbed up against its flow at the end of Inferno 34. Blind means dark.

context: She came down to Limbo and asked Virgil to rescue Dante, as Virgil told in Inferno 2.

quote: has never seen his final evening
note: He is still alive. Virgil means the death of the soul as well: Dante was close to being lost for good.
The dark forest of Inferno 1, where Dante had lost his way.

The key word of the canto. Cato died for political freedom. Dante is seeking freedom of the will, the soul no longer a slave to sin, and the climb of Purgatory is how it is won. At the top, in Canto 27, Virgil will tell him his will is free.
A city on the coast of North Africa, near Carthage. Cato killed himself there in 46 BC, when Caesar had won the civil war, rather than live under his rule.

quote: the flesh that will shine so bright
note: At the Last Judgment the souls will take back their bodies, and those of the blessed will shine. Virgil's words imply that Cato, a pagan and a suicide, will be saved. Dante never explains how.

context: Minos judges at the entrance to the second circle. Virgil's home, Limbo, is the first circle, above him and outside his power.
Virgil's own place in Hell, among the virtuous pagans.

Dante saw her among the noble Romans in Inferno 4. Lucan tells how Cato gave her to his friend Hortensius, and how after Hortensius died she begged Cato to take her back, so that she could die as Cato's wife.

note: The seven terraces of the mountain, one for each of the seven deadly sins. Cato is guardian of them all, though he stays at the foot.

context: Marcia is in Limbo, on the far side of it.

note: Cato died before Christ, so he too must have waited in Limbo. He is usually understood to have been taken out when Christ descended into Hell and freed the righteous (Inferno 4). From then on, nothing in Hell can touch the saved, not even love for a wife.
The reed stands for humility, the first thing needed for the climb. It replaces the cord Dante wore around his waist in Hell, which Virgil threw into the abyss in Inferno 16.
Dante's face is still marked by the grime of Hell and by his tears there. The washing is a small rite of cleansing before the mountain.

No angels have appeared in the poem so far, apart from the heavenly messenger who opened the gate of Dis in Inferno 9. The first one here is the boatman of Canto 2. Many commentators take Cato to mean the angel who guards the gate of Purgatory in Canto 9.
Purgatory is a mountain rising from an island, alone in the ocean of the southern hemisphere. It stands exactly opposite Jerusalem on the globe.
Only the reed lives where the waves strike, because it bends. Anything stiff, like pride, is broken.
In Purgatory the sun is the guide. The souls can climb only by daylight, as Canto 7 explains, and the poem keeps close track of the sun's position.
First light on Easter Sunday morning, 1300. Dante's Italian in these lines is famous for its last words, "il tremolar de la marina", the trembling of the sea.
Virgil wets his hands in the dew to wash Dante's face. Dew falling from the sky is an old image of God's grace.
Stained by the tears Dante shed for the damned, and perhaps by new ones now. Virgil's washing undoes what Hell did to him.

quote: whose waters have never been sailed
note: A glance back at Ulysses. In Inferno 26 he told how he sailed past the limits of the known world, came within sight of a great mountain, this one, and was sunk by a whirlwind before he could land.

Dante's Italian says "as pleased another". Ulysses used the same words, of God, for the storm that drowned him in Inferno 26. Dante reaches the shore Ulysses could not, because he comes in humility and with heaven's leave.

The reed grows back at once. In Aeneid 6, the golden bough Aeneas must pick before entering the underworld is replaced by another as soon as it is torn off. Dante turns the gold into a common rush: humility, like grace, is never used up.
